name: CScale
desc: Develops optical interconnect chips that link AI accelerators across racks in large data-centre compute clusters.
markets: Pre-revenue; first chips planned for 2028. Operations in Palo Alto, US; no verified international operations.
rationale: Pre-revenue chip developer selling to a few hyperscalers; little brand marketing need, though Nvidia and Intel backing adds tech profile.
changed: Emerged from stealth with Series C in September 2026

name: Glow
desc: Sells an AI-driven endpoint security platform that monitors and controls software, AI agents and developer tools on employee devices.
markets: Launched from stealth in July 2026; enterprise customer locations not disclosed. No verified international operations or expansion plans.
rationale: Newly launched security vendor competing with CrowdStrike, an F1 sponsor; possible later, but too early for a major sponsorship.

name: Chronograph
desc: Provides cloud portfolio monitoring, data collection and analytics software for private equity, venture and other private capital investors.
markets: Clients are US and international GPs and LPs; London office since 2023 serves international clients; plans further international growth.
rationale: Niche B2B fintech whose investor clients value hospitality; F1 event entertainment in the US and UK could support growth.
changed: Minority growth investment from Sixth Street in 2026

name: DeepInfra
desc: Runs an inference cloud that serves open-source AI models to developers and companies through an API on its own GPUs.
markets: Owns GPU infrastructure in eight US data centres and one in Toronto, Canada (2026); says further global locations are planned.
rationale: Developer-focused AI cloud; F1 could showcase speed and scale, but marketing budget and brand ambitions are still modest.

name: Eclypsium
desc: Sells firmware, hardware and supply chain security software for IT devices and infrastructure to enterprises and government agencies.
markets: Customers are US enterprises and government agencies; one database lists staff in 10 countries, unverified; earlier funding aimed at global expansion.
rationale: Niche B2B security vendor; limited brand marketing, though B2B hospitality could help reach enterprise and telecom buyers.

name: HiddenLayer
desc: Sells a security platform that protects machine learning models and AI agents from attacks, for enterprises and government.
markets: US enterprise and defence customers; international customers include a large pharma firm and automotive brands; expansion beginning in Europe.
rationale: Fast-growing AI security vendor with automotive and enterprise clients; F1 offers technology showcase and hospitality, though budget is limited.

name: Ocient
desc: Sells a hyperscale data warehouse and analytics software for very large datasets, used by telecom, adtech and government customers.
markets: Customers mainly in the US; 2026 partnership with Minsait to serve telecom and media companies in Brazil.
rationale: Data-heavy analytics platform could showcase F1 telemetry-scale processing, but a small B2B vendor with modest marketing.

name: Onyx Security
desc: Sells security software that lets enterprises monitor, govern and control the AI agents used across their organisations.
markets: Operates from New York and Tel Aviv, Israel; enterprise customer countries not disclosed; funds aimed at scaling go-to-market.
rationale: Early-stage AI security vendor; tech showcase possible, but too young for meaningful F1 spend.
changed: Launched in March 2026; Series B in July 2026

name: ORO Labs
desc: Sells an AI procurement orchestration platform that coordinates intake, approvals and buying tools for large enterprises.
markets: Staff in the US, India and Europe; London base; customers include Coca-Cola, Roche, Bayer, Stellantis and Siemens Energy.
rationale: Enterprise software selling to large multinationals; F1 hospitality could reach procurement and finance leaders in Europe and the US.

name: Prime Intellect
desc: Runs a compute marketplace and platform for distributed AI model training, reinforcement learning and agents, and releases open models.
markets: Serves developers and companies online from San Francisco; aggregates GPUs from many cloud providers; customer countries not disclosed.
rationale: Developer-focused AI infrastructure startup with little brand marketing; F1 fit is weak at this stage.

name: FITURE
desc: Sells smart fitness mirrors and connected home workout equipment with subscription classes to consumers in China.
markets: Customers and retail stores in Chinese cities; announced US and Europe plans around 2023 not verified; current status unconfirmed.
rationale: Chinese consumer fitness brand with domestic focus and reported layoffs; F1 fit weak unless overseas expansion is confirmed.

name: Cyxtera Technologies
desc: Data centre colocation operator whose assets were sold to Brookfield Infrastructure after its 2023 Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
markets: Brookfield bought seven US data centres; Canadian sites sold to Cologix and three international sites exited in 2024.
rationale: Former listed colocation firm now absorbed by Brookfield; no independent marketing budget, weak F1 fit.
changed: Filed for Chapter 11 in 2023; assets sold to Brookfield Infrastructure in 2023

name: Edgio
desc: Former content delivery network and edge security provider that ceased operations in January 2025 after bankruptcy.
markets: Defunct; no current customers. Contracts went to Akamai, Uplynk to its lender; French and Dutch subsidiaries dissolved.
rationale: Defunct company that ceased all operations in January 2025, with no brand, customers or budget; no F1 fit.
changed: Filed for Chapter 11 in September 2024; assets sold to Akamai and others; ceased operations January 2025

name: Sayari
desc: Provides corporate ownership, trade and sanctions risk intelligence data to banks, corporates and government agencies.
markets: Customers in 35+ countries including US agencies, HMRC and HSBC; offices in Washington, London, Canada, Israel and Dubai; Nordic-Benelux government push 2026.
rationale: Niche compliance data vendor selling to governments and banks; limited consumer marketing, though B2B hospitality could reach financial clients.

name: Zip
desc: Sells an AI procurement orchestration platform handling intake, approvals, sourcing, purchasing and supplier risk for enterprises.
markets: US-led customer base; offices in San Francisco, New York, Toronto and London; European customers include Arm and N26.
rationale: Fast-growing enterprise software brand courting CFOs and procurement leaders; F1 hospitality in the US and Europe is plausible.

name: Writer
desc: Sells an enterprise generative AI platform with its own Palmyra language models and agent tools to large companies.
markets: Offices in San Francisco, New York and London; enterprise customers include Uber, Spotify, L'Oreal and Accenture; pursuing international expansion.
rationale: Enterprise AI brand selling to marketing teams of global companies; F1 could showcase AI and host enterprise buyers.

name: Altana
desc: Runs an AI supply chain network mapping trade flows for customs authorities, logistics providers and manufacturers for compliance and risk.
markets: Customers include US federal agencies, the UK Department for Business and Trade and Maersk; offices in New York, Washington and London.
rationale: Government-heavy B2B data platform with little brand marketing; F1 logistics angle exists but fit is weak.

name: Avathon
desc: Sells industrial AI software for predictive maintenance, asset monitoring and autonomy to energy, manufacturing and defence customers.
markets: US-based with a large R&D hub in India; customers include BP, Hitachi High-Tech, the British Army and BAE Systems.
rationale: Industrial AI vendor to energy and defence firms; F1 could showcase predictive analytics, but brand marketing is limited.
changed: Renamed from SparkCognition to Avathon in 2024

name: Corelight
desc: Sells network detection and response software built on open-source Zeek to enterprises, financial institutions and government agencies.
markets: Customers include US and international government agencies and enterprises; European sales operations since 2019; took part in NATO exercise 2026.
rationale: Technical security vendor with niche brand; limited F1 fit beyond B2B hospitality for enterprise and government buyers.

name: Iru
desc: Sells an AI-powered device management and security platform for Apple, Windows and Android fleets to businesses.
markets: Over 6,000 customers globally; offices in California, Miami, London, Sydney and Japan, with Japan unit covering Korea.
rationale: IT software brand with customers in the US, Europe and Asia-Pacific; F1 offers B2B hospitality and brand building after rename.
changed: Renamed from Kandji to Iru in 2025

name: 0G Labs
desc: Develops a decentralized AI operating system with its own blockchain, data availability and storage layers for onchain AI apps.
markets: Mainnet live since September 2025; user and operator countries not disclosed; no verified international offices.
rationale: Crypto infrastructure project; crypto brands sponsor F1, but a developer-focused protocol has limited consumer marketing need.

name: Hex Technologies
desc: Sells a collaborative data analytics platform with notebooks, apps and AI agents used by data teams at companies.
markets: Says 2,500+ customers globally, mostly US technology firms; offices in San Francisco and New York; plans global expansion.
rationale: Data software brand for analysts; F1 data angle exists, but marketing scale and enterprise buyer reach are limited.

name: ChapsVision
desc: Sells data, AI, cybersecurity and intelligence software to governments, defence, security, finance and retail organisations.
markets: Over 2,000 customers in 40+ countries from seven offices, mainly Western Europe and the US; expanding in Nordics.
rationale: Acquisitive European software group seeking profile against Palantir; F1 could build brand with government and enterprise buyers.

name: Coro
desc: Sells a modular cybersecurity platform for small and midsize businesses, mainly through managed service providers and resellers.
markets: Offices in Chicago, New York, London, Madrid, Milan and Israel; staff in 11 countries; pursuing channel-driven global expansion.
rationale: SMB security vendor selling via partners in the US and Europe; F1 hospitality for channel partners is plausible but not obvious.
